note:
ISO 2026-W19 runs from May 4 through May 10. Venus is about 2.1° in ecliptic longitude from Aldebaran in Taurus.

**Naked eye:** 🌗 Last Quarter — 21:10:28 UTC. Moderate moonlight makes timing and local sky position important for faint targets. Use Denebola, Phecda as the week’s fixed-sky framework.

**Planets:** Moon: Naked eye; magnitude -11.9; direct motion; 95.1% illuminated. Below the horizon at 21:00 local apparent solar time, 45°N. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Conjunction with Pluto in ecliptic longitude May 08 18:21 UTC. Mercury: In solar glare; magnitude -1.0; direct motion; 90.7% illuminated. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Venus: Naked eye; magnitude -3.9; direct motion; 87.3% illuminated. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Mars: Naked eye; magnitude 1.2; direct motion; 97.6% illuminated. Below the horizon at 21:00 local apparent solar time, 45°N. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Ceres: In solar glare; magnitude 8.8; direct motion; 99.9% illuminated. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Jupiter: Naked eye; magnitude -2.0; direct motion; 99.2% illuminated. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Saturn: Naked eye; magnitude 0.9; direct motion; 99.9% illuminated. Below the horizon at 21:00 local apparent solar time, 45°N. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Uranus: In solar glare; magnitude 5.8; direct motion; 100.0% illuminated. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Neptune: Telescope; magnitude 7.8; direct motion; 100.0% illuminated. Below the horizon at 21:00 local apparent solar time, 45°N. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Pluto: Substantial telescope; magnitude 14.5; direct motion; 100.0% illuminated. Below the horizon at 21:00 local apparent solar time, 45°N. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Station May 06 15:34 UTC: turns retrograde. Conjunction with Moon in ecliptic longitude May 08 18:21 UTC.

**Binoculars:** Trace Virgo’s charted figure in the finder, then identify Zavijava at its charted position. Trace Hydra’s charted figure in the finder, then identify β Hya at its charted position. Trace Corvus’s charted figure in the finder, then identify Alchiba at its charted position.

**Small telescope:** MCG 8-22-2: consult its dedicated finder and observing story for equipment guidance; MCG 6-26-51: consult its dedicated finder and observing story for equipment guidance; M109: consult its dedicated finder and observing story for equipment guidance; MCG 9-20-52: consult its dedicated finder and observing story for equipment guidance; Antennae Galaxies: consult its dedicated finder and observing story for equipment guidance; Antennae Galaxies: consult its dedicated finder and observing story for equipment guidance; Arp 18: consult its dedicated finder and observing story for equipment guidance; MCG 7-25-26: consult its dedicated finder and observing story for equipment guidance

**Substantial telescope:** No fixed-sky Calendar object is classified as requiring a substantial telescope this week.

stories.dek: Alchiba is a star in Crv of catalogue visual magnitude 4.02; its declination determines which latitudes can observe it.
stories.body:
The stored catalogue gives a visual magnitude of 4.02. This is a catalogue value, not a prediction of its brightness this week. Lower magnitudes mean brighter objects; sky brightness and altitude affect whether you can see the star.

Its catalogue position is approximately right ascension 12h 08m and declination -24.7°. These reference coordinates describe its sky location; they are not an observing time or a current altitude.

At the almanac’s default latitude of 45° N, this star rises and sets, reaching approximately 20° altitude at upper culmination. These are geometric calculations from declination, excluding refraction and local obstructions. Darkness and the time of culmination must still be checked for the observing date and your location.

How to find it: Establish the preserved Crv constellation figure from its labeled reference stars, then use the target’s plotted position rather than searching for an isolated star.

Sources: Star Almanack’s stored fixed-object and expanded Bayer catalogues; accepted constellation figures and guiding-star routes. Visibility limits are original geometric calculations from catalogue declination, not weekly predictions.
